articles.title: Wrestling legend Ric Flair, 77, rushed to Tampa hospital after fall outside bar, head injuries: report
articles.summary: Ric Flair was reportedly rushed to a Tampa hospital by ambulance after falling outside a bar, suffering facial cuts and a possible concussion.
articles.body: Pro wrestling legend Ric Flair was reportedly rushed to a Florida hospital after falling outside a bar. According to TMZ, Flair was at a Tampa bar when he walked outside and fell, injuring his face and possibly suffering a concussion. TMZ says Flair cut his head and eye, which was bleeding, and was loaded into an ambulance. CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK SPORTS COVERAGE The reported fall came hours after Flair announced that he would be unable to attend a scheduled appearance in Seattle due to a blood clot in his leg. "My Doctors Have Limited My Travel To 3–4 Hours. Seattle Falls Outside That Range, And As Disappointed As I Am, I Have To Put My Health And Recovery First. Blood Clots Are Extremely Serious And Can Be Life-Threatening," Flair said on X. "We Have Seen This Recently With Jalen Hurts And The Complications Involving Blood Clots In His Lungs. It Is A Reminder That This Is Not Something To Take Lightly, And I Must Follow Medical Advice." Flair said he is slated to have surgery on the affected vein, "[w]hich My Doctors Expect Will Allow Me To Be Cleared For More Travel Afterward." "Please Know This Decision Was Not Made Lightly. I Am Truly Sorry For The Inconvenience And Disappointment, And I Am Incredibly Grateful For Your Patience, Understanding, And Continued Support. I Look Forward To Getting Healthy And Seeing You All Down The Road. Thank You For The Love And Support," Flair added. Tampa Fire Rescue told OutKick and Fox News Digital that it responded to a fall outside the establishment, and an adult male was taken to a local hospital — the department did not name Flair, saying they could not "provide any patient particulars due to HIPPA guidelines." Flair, 77, has battled health and alcohol issues over the years. EX-WRESTLER PAC'S SUDDEN DEATH CAUSE REVEALED BY COOK COUNTY MEDICAL EXAMINER'S OFFICE Flair has been in and out of wrestling for the last few years. His so-called "Last Match" took place in 2022 — a tag-team match with his then-son-in-law, the wrestler known as Andrade, against Jeff Jarrett and Jay Lethal. He later revealed he passed out twice during the match. Flair made his All Elite Wrestling debut in 2023 and was a brief part of Sting’s final professional match at AEW Revolution, where Sting and Darby Allin took on the Young Bucks. He was a World Championship Wrestling world heavyweight champion eight times, a National Wrestling Alliance world heavyweight champion nine times and a WWE champion twice during his career. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP The WWE inducted Flair into its Hall of Fame in 2008 as a singles wrestler and as a member of the Four Horsemen in 2012.

articles.title: Vanessa Trump 'finally cancer-free,' she says after health battle in emotional video with daughter Kai
articles.summary: Months after revealing her breast cancer diagnosis in April, Vanessa Trump announces she is cancer-free in an emotional video with daughter Kai Trump.
articles.body: Vanessa Trump revealed she is now cancer-free after battling breast cancer, sharing the emotional health update in a new video with her daughter, Kai Trump, months after publicly announcing her diagnosis. The 19-year-old granddaughter of President Donald Trump shared a preview of the conversation on Instagram during Breast Cancer Awareness Month, revealing that her mother, who's the ex-wife of Donald Trump Jr., was diagnosed in April. "And my mom was diagnosed with breast cancer in April, so we thought we'd share her story and how she was diagnosed, how she overcame it," Kai said in the video. KAI TRUMP REVEALS HOW FAMILY RALLIED AROUND MOM VANESSA AMID BREAST CANCER BATTLE: ‘IT’S A LONG JOURNEY’ To finish the social clip, Vanessa shared the news that she is now cancer-free. "And it came back clear, so I'm finally cancer-free," Vanessa said. "Love you!" Kai responded. The video also features former Fox News medical contributor Dr. Nicole Saphier, who discusses the importance of breast cancer awareness and early detection. "It feels different for everyone," Saphier said. "The reason I like social media talking about breast cancer is because it's reminding people that it is common." In her Instagram caption, Kai said she sat down with her mother and Saphier to discuss Vanessa's cancer journey, prevention and early detection. She also announced that the full conversation would be released on YouTube the following day. Vanessa, the mother of five, first revealed her breast cancer diagnosis in May. "I've recently been diagnosed with breast cancer," Vanessa wrote at the time. "While this isn't news anyone expects, I'm working closely with my medical team on a treatment plan." PRESIDENT'S 19-YEAR-OLD GRANDDAUGHTER, PICTURED IN HOSPITAL AFTER MEDICAL PROCEDURE She revealed that doctors had performed a procedure earlier that week and thanked her family for their support. "I am staying focused and hopeful while surrounded by the love and support of my family, my kids, and those closest to me," she wrote. The announcement prompted support from Ivanka Trump, who wrote, "Praying for your continued strength and a swift recovery. Love you mama." In June, Vanessa said she was recovering from surgery and preparing to begin the second stage of treatment, Fox News Digital reported. Kai Trump later opened up about the emotional experience in an August interview with Fox News Digital, shortly after beginning her freshman year at the University of Miami. CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER "There was definitely, there was a lot of crying in, like, the week leading up," she said of the days before leaving for college. "We would just be driving, and then we'd just start crying together." At the time, she said her mother was improving after treatment. "My mom, she's doing a lot better," she said. "Kind of after treatment, she wasn't feeling very good. Just like how treatment will make you feel … but she's getting a lot better now." Kai described the extra time she spent with her mother over the summer as a "blessing in disguise." "I was able to spend extra time with her that I would normally probably spend on the golf course," Kai said. "It was nice to spend those extra hours with her throughout the day before going to college." CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Now, months after Vanessa first revealed her diagnosis and Kai described their emotional summer together, the mother and daughter are sharing a hopeful new chapter. Fox News Digital's Sophia Compton and Paulina Dedaj contributed reporting.

articles.title: Corpo de homem desaparecido no Rio Branco é encontrado em Boa Vista | G1
articles.standfirst: Vítima desapareceu nesta sexta-feira (23) e foi encontrada sem vida neste sábado (24), perto da Orla Taumanan. Ele ainda não foi identificado.
articles.summary: Vítima desapareceu nesta sexta-feira (23) e foi encontrada neste sábado (24), perto da Orla Taumanan. Ele ainda não foi identificado.
articles.body:
Corpo de homem que estava desaparecido foi encontrado pelo Corpo de Bombeiros na manhã destes sábado (24). — Foto: Kailane Souza/Rede Amazônica

O corpo de um homem , ainda não identificado e que estava desaparecido, foi encontrado no Rio Branco, na manhã deste sábado (24), pelo Corpo de Bombeiros, em Boa Vista . As equipes localizaram a vítima sem vida por volta das 8h30 .

Ele estava desaparecido desde as 16h desta sexta-feira (23). Os bombeiros foram chamados e iniciaram as buscas na água logo em seguida. A operação de resgate parou às 18h de ontem e retornou nas primeiras horas de hoje.

A Rede Amazônica apurou que, até o momento, nenhum familiar procurou a corporação para pedir informações.

O corpo foi levado para o Instituto Médico Legal (IML), onde passará por exames para tentar confirmar a identidade.

articles.title: Negligência médica em Guarujá: mãe perde bebê e tem útero retirado | G1
articles.standfirst: Mulher afirma que houve demora no atendimento após a ausência de batimentos cardíacos do bebê ser identificada no hospital em Guarujá (SP). Após o parto, ela também passou por retirada do útero.
articles.summary: A Polícia Civil investiga denúncia de negligência no Hospital Santo Amaro após paciente perder o bebê e ter o útero retirado por demora no atendimento em Guarujá.
articles.body:
Ana Paula Cruz Santos alega negligência durante parto em hospital do Guarujá, SP. — Foto: Arquivo Pessoal

Uma mulher de 37 anos registrou um boletim de ocorrência por suspeita de negligência médica após dar à luz a um bebê natimorto no Hospital Santo Amaro, em Guarujá , no litoral de São Paulo. Ana Paula Cruz Santos alega que houve demora no atendimento após a identificação da ausência de batimentos cardíacos do bebê. Após o parto, ela também teve o útero retirado.

O parto ocorreu na madrugada de terça-feira (20). Ao g1 , Ana Paula contou que, no dia anterior (19), passou por uma consulta de pré-natal de alto risco na Casa Rosa , devido à hipertensão arterial crônica. Segundo ela, estava grávida de oito meses e com a pressão arterial em 17, motivo pelo qual foi encaminhada ao Hospital Santo Amaro. A Polícia Civil investiga o caso.

Segundo o relato, no hospital, a médica que atendeu Ana Paula ouviu os batimentos cardíacos do bebê e administrou um medicamento na veia para aliviar as cólicas. Segundo a mulher, foi solicitada uma ultrassonografia para a manhã seguinte, já que o exame não era realizado naquele horário. Ela também fez exames de sangue e urina, mas foi liberada.

Em nota, a Secretaria de Segurança Pública de São Paulo (SSP-SP) informou que o caso foi registrado como morte natural na Delegacia de Polícia de Guarujá, que requisitou exame pericial ao Instituto Médico Legal (IML) para esclarecimento dos fatos.

Procurado, o Hospital Santo Amaro não se posicionou sobre o caso até a última atualização desta reportagem.

De acordo com o relato, as dores aumentaram depois que chegou em casa e, por isso, voltou ao hospital por volta das 19h, acompanhada da mãe. Segundo ela, o médico que a atendeu tentou ouvir os batimentos do bebê, mas não conseguiu. A mulher afirmou que continuou sentindo fortes dores enquanto aguardava os resultados dos exames e passava por outros procedimentos.

“Ele colocou o aparelho na minha barriga e não escutou o coração do neném. [...] O que ele tinha que ter feito de imediato era uma cesárea de emergência”, disse ela.

Ana Paula contou que permaneceu no hospital durante a noite e que, por volta das 3h, começou a sangrar ao tentar ir ao banheiro . Em seguida, foi encaminhada para uma cesárea de emergência, mas o bebê nasceu morto.

Ana Paula disse que sofreu uma hemorragia e precisou receber transfusões de sangue. Ela também afirmou que teve seu útero retirado após a cesárea, o que a impossibilita de engravidar novamente. A mulher atribui o ocorrido à assistência recebida no hospital.

“Eu não tô conseguindo processar tudo isso, acabou para mim. Quem me conhece sabe que o sonho da minha vida era ser mãe. Está doendo demais o que fizeram comigo. Eu não vou poder ter filho mais e mataram meu filho”, disse.

Ana Paula relatou que tenta lidar com a perda do bebê e com a impossibilidade de ter outros filhos. “Meu peito enche de leite e eu não tenho filho para amamentar. Eu sinto o meu bebê mexer lá dentro, mas não tem bebê nenhum. Eu fiz uma cesárea e não tenho criança. Eles acabaram com o sonho da minha vida inteira de ter um filho”, afirmou.

articles.title: VÍDEOS mostram sujeira e armazenamento impróprio de órgãos no Base | G1
articles.standfirst: Denúncias atingem setor de autópsias e análises de material do Hospital de Base. Iges diz que imagens não refletem situação atual e que houve troca recente na gestão.
articles.summary: Iges diz que imagens não refletem situação atual pois houve troca na gestão do setor.
articles.body:
Funcionários e ex-funcionários do Hospital de Base, em Brasília , denunciam as condições precárias no setor de Anatomia Patológica, para onde vão corpos para autópsia, órgãos removidos durante cirurgias e materiais coletados para análise.

Vídeos mostram sujeira, falha na proteção dos trabalhadores e recipientes improvisados para armazenamento de órgãos ( veja detalhes abaixo ). Em uma das imagens, é possível ver que a tranca de gavetas onde ficam os corpos não fecham ( assista vídeo acima ). Por dentro da estrutura, muita sujeira.

Os funcionários dizem ainda que precisam usar equipamentos de proteção vencidos. No mês passado, uma reclamação foi registrada na ouvidoria do GDF por um funcionário que diz ser vítima de perseguição, constrangimento e condutas hostis.

Após questionamento, a reportagem foi convidada a conhecer o setor de Anatomia Patológica e encontrou uma situação diferente das imagens denunciadas ( veja mais detalhes no fim da reportagem ). Funcionários afirmam que houve uma grande faxina durante toda a madrugada anterior à visita.

Funcionários denunciam condições precárias no Hospital de Base, em Brasília — Foto: Reprodução

Outras imagens mostram o local de armazenamento de materiais biológicos, que já passaram ou vão passar por biópsia. É possível ver potes de plástico, inclusive de sorvete.

"A gente leva da nossa própria casa. A manteiga que a gente terminou de usar na copa vai para lá, para a gente poder usar e armazenar esses órgãos que a gente recebe do centro cirúrgico", disse um ex-funcionário que preferiu não se identificar.

Os órgãos que chegam ao setor são cedidos pelas famílias para serem usados na residência médica. No entanto, segundo o ex-funcionário, o protocolo de como deveria ser feito o armazenamento não é seguido .

"Tem fungo, ainda tem esse risco biológico", afirma.

O Instituto de Gestão Estratégica de Saúde do Distrito Federal (Iges) – que faz a gestão do Hospital de Base – afirmou à reportagem que as imagens não refletem como está o setor atualmente, já que houve uma mudança recente na gestão do setor .

A gerente-geral do Serviço de Diagnóstico de Imagem, Marlucy Mendes Soares, negou que a faxina feita no local teve relação com a ida da reportagem ao local . A gestora disse ainda que a limpeza é periódica e afirmou que não há irregularidade nas imagens feitas pelos funcionários.

"A resolução diz que o pote precisa estar fechado, identificado e a peça estar acondicionado com formol diluído em água. Todas as peças que foram mostradas no vídeo estavam nessas condições."

Marlucy Mendes Soares declarou ainda que as geladeiras passam por manutenção e limpeza com regularidade.

articles.standfirst: A previsão de conclusão é para o primeiro semestre de 2027.
articles.summary: Com 54% das obras concluídas, o Hospital Estadual de Itapetininga abre mais de 50 vagas na construção civil para contratação imediata via PAT.
articles.body:
As obras do Hospital Estadual do Alto Paranapanema, em Itapetininga (SP), chegaram a 54,89% de execução. Segundo a Secretaria de Estado da Saúde (SES), a previsão é de que a construção seja concluída no primeiro semestre de 2027. O investimento é de R$ 254,9 milhões.

Os trabalhos começaram em março de 2025 e, conforme a secretaria, seguem dentro do cronograma inicial.

Hospital Estadual do Alto Paranapanema será referência para 13 municípios da região e deve beneficiar cerca de 520 mil habitantes — Foto: Clara Abrami

O hospital será referência para 13 municípios da região e deve beneficiar cerca de 520 mil habitantes. De acordo com o projeto, a unidade terá 240 leitos, dos quais 44 serão destinados a cuidados intensivos e intermediários.

A estrutura também contará com pronto atendimento, centro cirúrgico, hospital-dia, ambulatório, serviço de quimioterapia, radioterapia Fe exames de diagnóstico.

Um carro capotou após uma colisão lateral com outro veículo na tarde deste sábado (24), na Avenida Princesa d'Oeste, em Campinas (SP). O uma mulher de 19 anos, que conduzia o carro que capotou, foi encaminhada ao Hospital São Luís com ferimentos leves.

Imagens de câmeras de segurança obtidas pela EPTV , emissora afiliada da TV Globo , registraram o momento do acidente.

No vídeo, um carro preto se preparava para fazer uma conversão quando atingiu lateralmente um veículo branco que seguia pela faixa à esquerda. Após a batida, o carro branco atingiu uma placa, capotou e parou sobre o canteiro da via.

Segundo a Polícia Militar, os agentes foram acionados para atender à ocorrência por volta das 15h. Até a última atualização desta reportagem, não havia informação sobre o estado de saúde da mulher socorrida ao hospital.

De acordo com a Emdec, agentes foram até o local para sinalizar e monitorar o trânsito. O veículo capotado aguarda ser removido.

articles.title: Câncer de mama: técnica de enfermagem vence doença e inspira pacientes | G1
articles.standfirst: Dorinha trabalha há mais de 15 anos no Hospital Mário Kroeff, referência no tratamento oncológico; após quimioterapia, cirurgia e radioterapia, ela voltou ao trabalho para compartilhar sua experiência com outros pacientes
articles.summary: Após vencer o câncer de mama, a técnica de enfermagem Dorinha retornou ao Hospital Mário Kroeff para compartilhar sua história de superação com os pacientes.
articles.body:
Maria das Dores da Silva, conhecida como Dorinha, passou anos cuidando de pacientes com câncer no Hospital Mário Kroeff, na Penha, Zona Norte do Rio. Técnica de enfermagem, ela acompanhava de perto os desafios do tratamento oncológico.

Aos 54 anos, porém, precisou enfrentar a doença do outro lado: recebeu o diagnóstico de câncer de mama e contou com o apoio de colegas de trabalho durante o tratamento, como mostrou o RJ2 .

A experiência mudou a forma como ela encara o trabalho e a relação com os pacientes. Depois de passar por quimioterapia, cirurgia e sessões de radioterapia, Dorinha voltou à rotina no hospital levando também o próprio relato de superação.

“Passei a vir forte. Fui dando mais testemunho para eles. Como eu consegui, eles também conseguem”, conta.

Técnica de enfermagem que cuida de pacientes com câncer enfrenta a doença com apoio de colegas e volta para inspirar — Foto: Reprodução/TV Globo

Para a enfermeira Maria Alice Rodrigues, que acompanhou a colega durante esse período, a força de Dorinha foi marcante.

“Quando é uma pessoa próxima e da área de saúde, que já cuidou de tanta gente e agora precisou ser cuidada, a aceitação dela foi perfeita”, afirma.

Maria Alice destaca ainda a disposição da técnica de enfermagem para enfrentar o tratamento.

“Essa força dela, que eu não sei de onde vem. Se eu passasse por esse processo, não sei se eu teria tanta força como a Dorinha tem”, diz.

Do cuidado aos pacientes à experiência com a doença

A rotina profissional de Dorinha já era marcada pelo contato com pessoas que enfrentavam o câncer. Quando recebeu o próprio diagnóstico, ela precisou passar pelas etapas do tratamento, com os desafios físicos e emocionais que acompanham o processo.

A volta ao trabalho ganhou um significado diferente. A técnica de enfermagem passou a dividir sua experiência com pacientes que enfrentam a mesma doença e a mostrar que é possível atravessar o tratamento.

“A gente tira uma força que só Deus mesmo. A gente nem imagina que tem essa força. Só de chegar no trabalho é uma vitória”, relata.

O oncologista Tiago Costa, que acompanha o caso, afirma que a doença está atualmente sob controle . Ele reforça a importância de procurar avaliação médica diante de alterações nas mamas.

“Quando notam um nódulo na mama, quando apalpa, pode ser um gatilho para fazer esses exames de ultrassonografia, de mamografia”, explica.

O médico também destaca os avanços no tratamento. “Não se intimide, não esmoreça, porque o tratamento hoje é eficaz. Então, tem plenas condições de tratar, assim como a Dorinha, e vencer o tratamento”, afirma.

Depois de enfrentar o tratamento, Dorinha viveu um momento simbólico: bateu o sino que representa a conclusão de uma etapa dessa jornada.

Ao falar sobre o significado do gesto, ela resume: “Vitória, momento de vitória, mais vida, mais experiência”.

A história da técnica de enfermagem ganha destaque durante o Outubro Rosa, campanha de conscientização sobre o câncer de mama que reforça a importância da prevenção, da atenção aos sinais do corpo e do diagnóstico precoce.

articles.title: Australian MP Helen Haines' condition improves after alleged car attack
articles.summary: The Independent MP is now in a serious but stable condition, according to the Melbourne hospital.
articles.body:
The condition of Helen Haines, the Australian MP hit by a car five days ago in north-east Victoria, has improved from critical to serious but stable.

The independent MP, 65, had both her legs amputated after what authorities say was a deliberate attack outside her electorate office in Wangaratta, north-east of Melbourne, on Monday.

In the latest update on Saturday morning, the Alfred Hospital in Melbourne said Haines was in a serious but stable condition, the first improvement since she was airlifted there.

Her alleged attacker, 43-year-old Brendan Nugent, was arrested shortly after the incident and has since appeared in court on three charges.

The politician's husband, Phil Haines, said on Wednesday that the "horrendous incident" had caused his wife significant injuries but "her heart and her mind" were "in good shape".

Nugent, who was arrested moments after he allegedly drove his Toyota LandCruiser into the MP, appeared in court to face three charges: dangerous driving causing serious injury, intentionally causing serious injury, and causing harm to a Commonwealth public official.

Police said more charges might be laid, including attempted murder.

His lawyer said his client had "mental health concerns" but did not give any further detail.

Victoria Police has said its investigation, with support from the Australian Federal Police, remains ongoing and a motive is yet to be established.

Investigators are looking into whether drug use or medication played a part in the incident.

Nugent's family has said they were long-time friends with Haines.

Shortly after the alleged attack, Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese told ABC television that there had been a "rise in temperature" and "too much shouting, not enough discourse" in Australia.

Haines, known for stances such as supporting stronger climate action, entered parliament in 2019 after working as a nurse and midwife.

articles.title: 450 people in Gorakhpur receive anti-rabies shots after consuming charanamrit made from suspected rabid cow’s milk; Hyderabad doctor explains whether rabies can spread through milk and when vaccination is necessary
articles.summary: The news of around 450 people receiving anti-rabies vaccinations in Uttar Pradesh’s Gorakhpur district has raised an important public health question: can
articles.body: The news of around 450 people receiving anti-rabies vaccinations in Uttar Pradesh’s Gorakhpur district has raised an important public health question: can drinking milk from a cow suspected of having rabies expose people to the deadly infection?According to reports, people from two villages received vaccinations after consuming charanamrit, a religious offering prepared using milk from a cow that reportedly displayed unusual behaviour and died after a suspected stray dog bite.Can rabies spread through milk?Dr Sudhir Kumar, a Hyderabad-based physician, has clarified that rabies transmission through milk has not been demonstrated in humans. He also noted that consuming milk or milk products alone does not generally call for rabies post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP).Rabies is usually transmitted when the saliva of an infected animal enters the body through a bite, scratch, broken skin or the moist lining of the eyes, nose or mouth. Drinking milk is not an established route of human rabies transmission.However, this does not make raw milk from a suspected rabid animal safe to consume. Avoid it and seek medical advice if there may have been direct contact with the animal’s saliva.Why did hundreds of people receive vaccinations?Rabies is almost always fatal once symptoms develop, making suspected exposures a serious public health concern. Health authorities may take precautionary action while investigating a possible exposure, particularly when many people are involved.The Gorakhpur vaccination drive does not establish that the milk transmitted the virus. Nor does it confirm that the cow had rabies.A similar precautionary response followed reports of people consuming unpasteurised milk from rabid cows in Massachusetts in the 1990s. Such responses reflect caution around a potentially deadly disease, not proof of transmission through milk.When is an anti-rabies vaccine necessary?Rabies PEP may be needed after a bite or scratch from a suspected infected animal, or when its saliva directly contacts broken skin or the eyes, nose or mouth.Anyone who experiences such contact should wash the affected area thoroughly with soap and running water for 15 minutes and seek urgent medical assessment. Depending on the exposure, treatment may include rabies vaccination and rabies immunoglobulin.A person who has only consumed milk should not automatically assume vaccination is necessary. A healthcare professional must assess any additional exposure, including possible contact with saliva.Does boiling milk destroy the rabies virus?Heat can inactivate the rabies virus, and properly boiled milk is not considered an established route of rabies transmission. Nevertheless, raw milk can carry other disease-causing germs, so pasteurised or properly boiled milk is the safer choice.Avoid consuming milk from an animal suspected of having rabies, even if it appears normal. If exposure is uncertain, consult a doctor rather than relying on home treatment or assumptions about cooking.What should people remember?The key lesson from Gorakhpur is to separate precaution from confirmed transmission. The reported vaccination drive does not prove that rabies passed through the religious offering.Rabies prevention depends on recognising genuine exposure, washing wounds immediately and seeking timely medical care. Anyone worried about a possible contact should explain exactly what happened to a healthcare professional.

articles.title: Hospital in Yemen’s Taiz warns of collapse in days because of Houthi siege
articles.summary: Dialysis patients face shorter treatment sessions as severe shortages of fuel, medicines, and oxygen threaten hospitals.
articles.body:
Taiz, Yemen – It was approaching 10:30am in the dialysis centre of the Republican Hospital in Taiz when a machine began filtering excess fluids, toxins and salts from the blood of Omar Mukhtar Hammoud.

The 16-year-old suffers from kidney failure and is one of 270 patients who regularly receive dialysis at the centre in the government-held city in southwest Yemen. But with essential medical supplies and fuel running critically low under the renewed Houthi siege , doctors fear they may soon be unable to provide the treatment that keeps their patients alive.

Dr Essam Mahyoub Dahan, the centre’s director, warned that a complete shutdown could happen within days.

“Because of the siege and the shortage of diesel and medical solutions, we have recently been forced to reduce dialysis sessions from four hours to just two and a half,” Dahan told Al Jazeera. “We know this is not adequate, but we have no choice if we are to keep the centre operating for as long as possible before it shuts down completely.”

Dahan said the centre’s remaining stocks of specialised dialysis solutions were also close to running out.

The supplies, which are expensive, are normally provided by the Yemeni Ministry of Health every three months. But the latest delivery which was due earlier this month failed to arrive because of the Houthi siege on Taiz city. It began in the first week of October after Houthi advances in the Taiz countryside.

The city was previously under complete Houthi siege between 2015 and 2016, in the early years of Yemen’s ongoing war.

Across Taiz governorate, where battles are raging between the Saudi-backed Yemeni government forces and Iranian-allied Houthi fighters, the number of patients at risk is far greater.

In an October 12 statement, the governorate’s health office warned that the continued siege and obstruction of essential supplies could endanger the lives of 1,110 patients with kidney failure. They depend on dialysis services in the governorate’s hospitals, which collectively provide about 210 dialysis sessions a day.

International humanitarian and health organisations have issued similar warnings about the impact of the siege on the already fragile healthcare system in Taiz.

On Thursday, Amnesty International called on the Houthis to immediately reopen vital roads into and around the city, warning that the closure of the main road between Taiz and the southern port city of Aden threatened hundreds of thousands of civilians with losing access to food, water and healthcare.

Taiz’s hospitals depend heavily on diesel-powered generators because much of the city’s electricity infrastructure was destroyed during the war that began 11 years ago and has not been restored.

The renewed Houthi siege has severely disrupted the entry of fuel, including the diesel needed to run hospital generators and lifesaving medical equipment.

Dr Shaheed al-Ameri, deputy director-general for technical affairs at the Republican Hospital, said the shortages have had a devastating impact on medical services.

“A very large part of this suffering is because of the shortage of diesel,” he told Al Jazeera. “We have no reserve diesel supplies. Our stocks ran out early in the siege and we are now buying it on the black market almost every day, at prices that have reached five times what they were before the siege.”

Al-Ameri warned that the longer the siege continues, the more prices will rise and the further medical services will deteriorate.

The hospital has already suspended operations in some departments, including essential units, he said.

“If this situation continues much longer, we fear we will reach a complete and comprehensive collapse of healthcare services,” he said.

The shortages are not confined to the Republican Hospital. On October 22, the World Health Organization (WHO) warned that critical shortages of fuel, oxygen, medicines and medical supplies were threatening lifesaving healthcare throughout Taiz governorate, with some hospital services already disrupted.

According to the WHO, 42 health facilities in Taiz city had reported severe shortages of essential supplies. Hospitals and ambulances require at least 156,000 litres of fuel a month to continue functioning.

The organisation also warned that diesel shortages threaten to disrupt oxygen production, water pumping, vaccine refrigeration and sanitation services, increasing the risks of disease outbreaks, particularly among displaced families and other vulnerable groups.

The United Nations has separately warned that the restrictions on supplies are bringing Taiz’s health system close to collapse and urged the Houthis to allow humanitarian assistance and essential goods to enter without obstruction.

In its October 12 statement, Taiz’s health office warned that continued restrictions on fuel deliveries could lead to the shutdown of medical oxygen production plants, further endangering patients.

Taysir al-Samei, the health office’s media officer, said that would dramatically worsen the crisis.

“Many medical departments depend on oxygen, particularly operating theatres, inpatient wards, intensive care units and incubators for premature babies,” al-Samei said.

“Most hospitals have already suspended services in some units because of the shortage of diesel and the lack of necessary medical solutions, as well as shortages of medical staff who are struggling to get to work because of the lack of transport,” he added.

He warned that if conditions continued to deteriorate at the same pace, some hospitals could stop providing services in the coming days.

At the Republican Hospital, al-Ameri said that shortages were also affecting diagnostics and treatment. The availability of laboratory reagents had fallen to just 10 to 15 percent of previous levels, he said, while approximately half of the medicines normally available were now out of stock.

Prices for the remaining medicines had doubled, he said, placing them further out of reach for patients already struggling with Yemen’s worsening economic crisis.

The continued fighting and shelling around Taiz have increased the number of wounded people requiring emergency care – placing additional pressure on facilities already struggling with shortages of surgical supplies , anaesthetics and intravenous fluids.

Abdul Badi Abdulwuhab, 53, is another dialysis patient in the Republican Hospital, struggling to cope with the shorter dialysis sessions.

“Because of these measures, I suffer from weakness and I cannot bear the pain,” Abdul Badi told Al Jazeera. “Two and a half hours is not enough to remove all the fluids and toxins from my body.”

Dr Dahan said that the patient’s condition had deteriorated since his sessions were shortened.

“These measures are not effective for many patients,” Dahan said. “The only solution is to end the siege and return things to the way they were.”

articles.title: Northumberland disabled dance school struggling despite demand
articles.summary: Kate Stanforth needs to raise £20,000  to keep academy running and make dance 'genuinely accessible'.
articles.body:
A disabled-led dance school is struggling to keep running because of hidden costs and a lack of funding.

Kate Stanforth set up the Kate Stanforth Academy of Arts, working with dancers with a wide variety of disabilities and access requirements, during the pandemic, streaming classes online for free.

The 32-year-old, from Northumberland, said the classes were so popular she carried on, with the academy becoming a Community Interest Company (CIC) in 2023.

Most classes have continued online in order to remain accessible for all dancers and maintain equal opportunities.: "I know how devastating it feels to lose something you love because the world isn't built to include you," said Stanforth.

Stanforth began ballet classes at the age of two, but was left disabled at14 and believed her dancing days were over.

Eventually, she found her way back into the dance studio and discovered "dance didn't have to look the way I'd always been taught".

Now an ambulatory wheelchair-user, she has spent more than 15 years developing and refining her own adaptive dance practice.

"When I became disabled, I went from being a dancer with professional ambitions to feeling like there was no longer a place for me," Stanforth said.

"It wasn't because I'd lost my passion, creativity or ability to perform, but because the opportunities weren't accessible."

The dancer, who is also a resident dance artist at Great Ormond Street Hospital in London, said her main goal was to make sure disabled people were taken seriously as dancers.

So far, she has supported more than 500 dancers and worked with organisations including the The Royal Ballet School, receiving national recognition for her work on accessibility and inclusivity.

Stanforth said she had deliberately kept her dance classes discounted because she was mindful of the financial struggles faced by many disabled people, but, as a CIC, funding had become a significant struggle.

She said she wanted to expand in-person opportunities, but accessible venues and the subsequent fees for travel and equipment are "incredibly expensive".

Currently, she is trying to raise £20,000 to allow her to keep the academy running.

"We're not struggling because there isn't a need for what we do," Stanforth said.

"We're struggling because making dance genuinely accessible costs money, and those costs aren't always recognised."

While she is thrilled some of her dancers have moved onto professional opportunities, Stanforth said the classes were about more than that.

"We've also seen people find joy in movement again after believing that part of their life was over," she said.

"I don't want another generation of disabled dancers growing up believing their ambitions are unrealistic."

articles.title: Woman's life transformed when she rejected fast food and vowed to eat what she grows
articles.summary: From fast food to garden-to-table living, Carmen Perr shares her best tips for shopping at farmers markets and cooking with seasonal fresh herbs.
articles.body: Before Carmen Perr was sharing garden-to-table recipes with millions of people, she grew up in a busy household with lots of mouths to feed. "I grew up eating fast food," Perr, the youngest of six children, told Fox News Digital. Now a Los Angeles-based creator known as Carmen in the Garden, Perr began honing her green thumb more than a decade ago while working in real estate acquisitions. AMERICANS ARE MAKING COSTLY GROCERY MISTAKE EVEN BEFORE ENTERING THE STORE, EXPERT WARNS "I started gardening in my first corporate job as a way to cope with stress and anxiety, and I started with just a few potted herbs," she said. "I didn't know what I was doing, but then it slowly grew over time." Eventually, as she gained more space, her garden expanded to include fruits and vegetables, prompting her to learn how to cook with ingredients she had never used before. FROM YELLOWSTONE TO YOSEMITE, NEW COOKBOOK REVEALS RECIPES INSPIRED BY AMERICA'S MOST ICONIC PARKS "I had never cooked an artichoke until I grew one," she said. Those lessons paved the way for her forthcoming debut cookbook, "Cook What Grows: Seasonal Recipes & Gardening Wisdom for Everyday Eating." Perr said the book's roughly 100 recipes aim to "spotlight fresh produce in super flavorful but attainable ways." GROCERY SHOPPERS MAY BE RELYING ON A 'MISLEADING' CLUE WHEN CHOOSING HEALTHY FOODS "I think that there's a big misconception that eating seasonally has to be expensive," Perr said. "But when you go to a farmers market or your local grocery store, typically what's in season is the more inexpensive option." She recommends using your senses to guide your produce picks: Look for vibrant colors, feel whether an item is firm or soft and check that herbs smell fragrant. "When you pick up a bunch of cilantro, you should immediately be able to smell it," Perr said. Herbs can do much more than finish a dish, she added. Fresh, dried and even seeded forms of the same herb can taste totally different, so Perr encourages home cooks to experiment rather than follow strict rules. She uses fresh oregano steeped in hot oil with feta and makes dill-marinated chicken wings finished with dill salt and a dill dipping sauce. "You are getting a full dill immersion in a chicken wing format," she said. articles.title: Christina Applegate's MS misdiagnosis after 5 years of treatment exposes alarming medical reality
articles.summary: Christina Applegate's MS misdiagnosis highlights how brain lesions and common symptoms can mislead doctors, with nearly one in five referrals wrong.
articles.body: Christina Applegate’s recent revelation that she was misdiagnosed with multiple sclerosis is raising questions about how the disease can be confused with other conditions — even after years of treatment. The actress, 54, shared the news during an Oct. 20 episode of her podcast, "MeSsy," alongside co-host Jamie-Lynn Sigler, saying she was in a complete "state of shock." Applegate was first diagnosed with MS in 2021 after experiencing debilitating symptoms and undergoing extensive testing, including brain and spinal MRIs and a spinal tap. She said doctors found dozens of lesions on her brain. CHRISTINA APPLEGATE SAYS SHE WAS MISDIAGNOSED WITH MS AND IS NOW 'BACK AT SQUARE ONE' After years of treatment, her doctor decided to stop her regular infusions and monitor her B cells. "And my B cells didn't change. They didn't go higher, they didn't go lower, they didn't change, and she had never seen that. So I guess that began kind of a study into my diagnosis," Applegate shared. After additional brain scans, the doctor came into Applegate’s room and said, "Congratulations, you don't have MS." The actress did not consider this to be good news, however. "Because you don't get misdiagnosed and then all of a sudden [you’re] better," she said. "I haven't gotten better … If anything, I've gotten worse in some ways." CARLY SIMON REVEALS THE COMMON CONDITION THAT MASKED HER PARKINSON'S DIAGNOSIS Applegate noted that she has "every symptom" of someone with MS, adding that there are many conditions that mirror the disease. "There is no single element in the diagnostic process that tells you with 100% certainty that it is MS." She recalled that her MRIs clearly showed around 30 lesions, but said her neurologist identified a different feature — which she described as a "string" — that led to the conclusion that she did not have MS. "So I'm back at square one [and] don't know what's going on with me." Why MS can be misdiagnosed Dr. Marwa Kaisey, an associate professor of neurology at Cedars-Sinai in Los Angeles, said during a follow-up "MeSsy" podcast episode that misdiagnosis of MS is "fairly common." In a study of patients referred to MS clinics at UCLA and Cedars-Sinai, Kaisey — who has not treated Applegate — said she found that nearly one in five who arrived with an MS diagnosis ultimately did not have the disease. BRAIN TUMOR FOUND DURING PREVENTIVE SCAN PUTS FULL-BODY MRIS BACK IN THE SPOTLIGHT "Some [had been diagnosed] for decades," she said. "And a majority of them were on medication to treat their MS." The primary challenge, according to the doctor, is that there is no single test for MS. "It's not like we have something like a pregnancy test that says, yes, you have it, no, you don't." Instead, Kaisey said, "It's a list of criteria, some of which remain a little bit subjective." New clues on brain scans Most misdiagnosed patients did have some type of white matter spots, or lesions, on their MRI scans, Kaisey noted, but they had a different cause that was not MS. Newer imaging techniques may help doctors distinguish MS lesions from white matter spots caused by other conditions. Kaisey pointed to the "central vein sign," an MRI finding that looks for small blood vessels running through the center of lesions, which is a characteristic associated with MS. The sign was incorporated into updated MS diagnostic criteria to help doctors determine whether white matter lesions are consistent with the disease. Richard Ransohoff, MD, a Boston-based neurologist who sits on the Board of Directors for the American Brain Foundation, called the central vein sign "a real step forward" in distinguishing MS lesions from other abnormalities. "Things are getting better, and even in the time that Ms. Applegate has been having her symptoms and her evaluation, things have gotten better," said Ransohoff, who also has not treated the actress. SELMA BLAIR'S LAWYER CITES MISSED MEDICATION, HEAD INJURY AFTER IN-FLIGHT ARREST: WHAT DOCTORS SAY Many of the symptoms of MS — such as tingling or numbness in the feet, fatigue and brain fog — are very common in other conditions as well, according to both neurologists. "To distinguish MS from its mimics can be challenging, and doctors, even with the best intentions … can sometimes still get it wrong," Kaisey said. "To diagnose MS, we need a symptom that's kind of very specific to MS, and we also need the MRI that looks like MS." Kaisey said she has found that being "undiagnosed" with MS can be even harder than receiving the initial diagnosis, particularly when the disease has become intertwined with someone's identity, family and community. "So to suddenly take that away, I think it’s earth-shattering. It's life-changing in a huge way." EARLY PARKINSON’S SYMPTOMS MISDIAGNOSED FOR YEARS, TERRY CREWS’ WIFE REVEALS The neurologist emphasized that patients should feel comfortable asking questions and getting a second opinion. "Don't be afraid to do that, especially if something inside is telling you that you need to dig a little deeper," she advised. MS-mimicking conditions Ransohoff reiterated that MS misdiagnoses are common. "It’s a tough diagnosis, and there is no single element in the diagnostic process that tells you with 100% certainty that it is MS," he told Fox News Digital. The neurologist said even after a diagnosis, doctors should "keep an open mind" and be willing to reconsider. You simply have to say there are certain things we know and certain things we don't know." Classic early MS symptoms tend to appear relatively quickly, persist for weeks and then recede, according to Ransohoff. Anything producing a similar pattern can potentially mimic the disease. Some of those conditions may include certain strokes in younger people, neuromyelitis optica spectrum disease (a rare autoimmune disease of the central nervous system), MOG antibody disease (a rare autoimmune inflammatory disorder), lupus and migraine, he said. Kaisey noted that migraine can also produce MRI abnormalities in the form of white spots, although they are usually smaller and in a different shape and location. "Facing the unknown when you feel crappy is a very tough road to go." "If you're not looking closely at the MRI or you don't know exactly what to look for, you can confuse the two," she said. In some cases, reversing an MS diagnosis can actually provide a concrete alternative diagnosis and better-targeted treatment — but that did not happen in Applegate’s case, Ransohoff noted. "Facing the unknown when you feel crappy is a very tough road to go." Specialized care To prevent misdiagnosis, Ransohoff recommends that everyone who receives a multiple sclerosis diagnosis is seen by a specialist at a specialty MS center, who has developed pattern recognition after many occurrences of seeing the disease. The neurologist noted that MS treatment has advanced dramatically over the course of his career, growing from virtually no options to more than 20 medications today. "You want to work with someone who has experience with all those medicines, with all the various patterns that MS can show, because every person's MS is different," he said. If a treatment isn’t helping or is causing significant side effects, an MS specialist can reassess the approach and help identify a more appropriate medication, Ransohoff added. "If the diagnosis is correct and the treatment is correct, then they should do pretty well with their MS."

articles.title: Hunters and ranchers enlisted in battle against spread of flesh-eating parasite
articles.summary: A hunter's elk kill in Pecos County revealed the first confirmed U.S. wildlife case of New World screwworm, as USDA urges ranchers to watch for signs.
articles.body: A flesh-eating parasite that can harm cattle was found in an elk in western Texas, prompting officials to ask hunters and ranchers to help stop its spread. The U.S. Department of Agriculture said Wednesday that New World screwworm was found in an elk on a game ranch in Pecos County. A hunter reported the animal after killing it. The USDA and the Texas Parks and Wildlife Department (TPWD) are conducting additional wildlife surveillance, while the Texas Animal Health Commission plans to modify an existing infested zone. AMERICA'S BEEF SUPPLY SHRINKS AS CATTLE FARMER WARNS 'THE NUMBERS ARE JUST NOT HERE ANYMORE' "Hunters and others who spend time outdoors near infested areas are often among the first people to encounter affected wildlife, making their observations especially valuable to surveillance and response efforts," the USDA said in a statement. "As hunting seasons continue across Texas and other states, hunters are encouraged to stay alert for signs of NWS when observing, harvesting, or processing wildlife," it continued. PRICE OF ONE GRILLING STAPLE REMAINS AT RECORD HIGH AS BEEF LOVERS ADAPT It urged hunters to be on the lookout for visible maggots in wounds or body openings, open or enlarging wounds, foul-smelling injuries, and animals that appear weak or distressed, and to report anything suspicious promptly. Infection signs around the nose, mouth, ears, eyes or genital areas also warrant attention, the agency added. The TPWD urged hunters to inspect harvested animals before field dressing or moving them, and to also look out for irritated or depressed behavior, loss of appetite, head shaking, a smell of decaying flesh or unusual isolation in animals. CLICK HERE FOR MORE LIFESTYLE NEWS New World screwworm was eliminated from the U.S. decades ago, but the parasite has been moving north through Central America and Mexico, Fox News Digital previously reported. Last year, the U.S. halted livestock imports from Mexico to keep it out. The pause lasted more than a year, straining cattle supply and contributing to record-high beef prices. Reopening began in stages in August. TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ In June, officials confirmed the parasite in a Texas calf. They later found it in other animals, including a horse and a dog. The Texas elk was the first confirmed U.S. wildlife case in the current outbreak. "The partnership between TPWD biologists and local hunters and landowners expedited the identification and confirmation of this new detection," Texas wildlife division director Alan Cain said in a statement. Animals within that zone must be inspected and, if necessary, treated before being moved. The parasite is a threat to animal health and meat production, but the USDA says it does not affect food safety, according to reports. articles.title: Great relationships have 3 essential ingredients — and one factor that can ruin everything
articles.summary: Simon Sinek reveals his "3+1" formula for great relationships, breaking down why infatuation and dopamine spikes can send dangerously wrong signals.
articles.body: The difference between a good relationship and a great relationship could boil down to one formula. Simon Sinek, author, inspirational speaker and founder of The Optimism Company in New York, shared his breakdown of core compatibilities for successful couples. Sinek, who has built a following of millions with content about leadership and interpersonal communication, said he developed his "3+1" formula after years of considering what makes partnerships work. 5 MARRIAGE MISTAKES COUPLES MAKE WITHOUT REALIZING IT — AND HOW TO AVOID THEM The formula centers on the following three core factors that can ebb and flow over the course of a partnership. He also added a fourth bonus factor: circumstances. Being intellectually compatible with your partner is essential, Sinek told Fox News Digital. "You get along, you enjoy going out with them," he said. "It doesn't mean you're as smart as each other; it means you have something to talk about when you go out together." COMMON MARRIAGE HABIT COULD QUIETLY KILL YOUR SEX LIFE, EXPERT WARNS Emotional compatibility means being vulnerable and emotionally available to each other, while creative and sexual compatibility reflects enjoying intimacy with a partner. Sinek said he groups sexual attraction and creativity together, as they use the "same part of the brain" that is imaginative. "When people can bring imagination to their sex lives, that is creativity," he said. "You hear it in couples who have been together for 10, 15, 20 years – they talk about how things get stale, get boring. That's creativity." A good relationship can blossom with one-and-a-half or two of these factors, according to Sinek, but a great relationship includes all three. NEARLY 1 IN 3 MARRIED AMERICANS AREN'T HAVING SEX — EXPERT REVEALS HOW TO BRING BACK THE SPARK "They're not all on high at the same time, so they sort of need each other to get through the relationship," he said. The bonus factor – circumstances – is controlled by external forces and can tip the scales of a successful relationship, Sinek added. "Sometimes, we meet somebody who fits all three, but they live on the other side of the world, and we can't move our lives and they can't move theirs," he said. "Or maybe they're already in a relationship and you shrug your shoulders and say, 'Bad timing.'" "Sometimes we get infatuated because we find one or two of those things, but for it to really last, I’ve learned it takes all three, plus the circumstances." Mistaking infatuation for compatibility Sinek warned that having one or two of these factors so highly developed, especially early in a relationship, can create the misleading impression that "this is my person." CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "One of the biggest things I’ve learned about relationships is the danger of infatuation," Sinek said, noting that early attraction can be driven by dopamine rather than love at first sight. He said people can fall for "the fantasy that the person represents" and think, "I’ve been looking for someone like you for my whole life," despite knowing someone for only a few hours. After the initial infatuation fades, it may become more clear whether a person is a good long-term match, according to Sinek. He suggested that a lack of intense infatuation at the beginning could sometimes be a positive sign. "You hear about people who knew each other for 10 years because they worked together," he said. "And then they finally realize that they're in love with each other. There was no infatuation. There was no spike." CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER Sinek encourages people to give potential partners who meet many of the desired criteria a chance, even if there isn't an immediate spark. "I know I've made this mistake a million times," he said. "I met great people, but there was no infatuation, so I was like, ‘nope, not for me.’ Or I was seduced by the infatuation." Striking a balance For committed or long-term couples who seem to have the core factors out of balance, Sinek urges them to pay closer attention to habits that may be pulling them away from the relationship. "You see people who go out for dinner on a regular basis, and they are either on their phones the whole time, or they're looking in other directions," he said. CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES "Maybe somebody needs to put in an effort to say, ‘Let's put our phones away. Let's trade phones when we go out so we don't even have the temptation,’" Sinek suggested. The expert reiterated that for those who want a lasting relationship — in a fast-paced dating climate that’s more sexually driven and tied to instant gratification — all three parts of the formula must develop. "Sometimes we get infatuated because we find one or two of those things, but for it to really last, I’ve learned it takes all three." "Even the sexual connection sometimes doesn’t happen at the beginning, and that also can come later," he said. Emotional connection can change the dynamic between partners, Sinek added. He cautioned against placing too much importance on one or two factors simply because they are especially strong or appear early. TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ Sinek continued, "It’s recognizing that when they start to wax and wane, all three of them are going to matter and they’re going to show up naturally at some point, so it's more of an awareness rather than trying to force it."

articles.title: Jalen Hurts puts spotlight on blood thinners: 5 mistakes that could put patients at risk
articles.summary: Jalen Hurts' blood clot diagnosis puts blood thinners in the spotlight. Experts reveal five critical mistakes patients on anticoagulants must avoid.
articles.body: Philadelphia Eagles quarterback Jalen Hurts' diagnosis of blood clots in both lungs has put blood thinners in the spotlight. Hurts is receiving treatment with the medication and is expected to miss the remainder of the 2026 season, according to the NFL. Even young, physically active people can develop dangerous blood clots, especially when risk factors such as an injury, long travel or recent surgery combine. "Being in shape lowers your risk, but it doesn’t make you immune," said Dr. Joseph V. Lombardi, chief physician executive at AtlantiCare. CHRISTINA APPLEGATE'S MS MISDIAGNOSIS AFTER 5 YEARS OF TREATMENT EXPOSES ALARMING MEDICAL REALITY Hurts’ case also highlights the precautions patients taking blood thinners may need to follow. The medication can help prevent dangerous clots from growing or forming but can also make it harder for the body to stop bleeding after an injury — a concern for athletes playing high-contact sports or anyone who falls or gets hurt. "Taking [blood thinners] consistently, understanding potential interactions, and recognizing warning signs can greatly reduce the risk of complications," Dr. Yazan Abou-Ismail, a hematologist and thrombosis expert at the University of Utah, told Fox News Digital. STACKING SUPPLEMENTS WITHOUT KEY TEST CAN DO MORE HARM THAN GOOD, EXPERT WARNS Here are five mistakes patients should avoid: 1. Stopping treatment without medical guidance While some patients only need blood thinners for a limited time, others may need them long term. When a clot has a clear cause, such as an injury, treatment often lasts about three months, Lombardi told Fox News Digital. The duration depends on factors including the reason for treatment and whether a patient has had previous clots, Abou-Ismail added. Stopping too soon can raise the risk of another clot, while continuing longer than prescribed may increase bleeding risk. SILENT INFLAMMATION COULD BE DAMAGING YOUR BODY — AND 5 HABITS MAY HELP KEEP IT IN CHECK Patients should not stop or extend treatment without speaking with their doctor. 2. Skipping or doubling doses Missing doses repeatedly can weaken a medication's protection against clots, Abou-Ismail said, but what to do after a missed dose depends on the specific drug. Patients should follow the instructions for the prescription or call their pharmacist or doctor — not automatically take an extra dose to make up for a missed one. CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES 3. Adding medications or supplements without checking Aspirin and NSAIDs including ibuprofen can increase bleeding risk when taken with blood thinners, Abou-Ismail said. Some prescription drugs and supplements, including fish oil and turmeric, can also affect bleeding or medication levels. Patients should ask a doctor or pharmacist before taking anything new, even if it is sold over the counter. 4. Brushing off signs of serious bleeding Some bruising or minor bleeding may occur but persistent nosebleeds, blood in the urine or unexplained increases in bruising warrant a call to a health care provider, Abou-Ismail said. CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER Uncontrolled bleeding, vomiting blood, black or tarry stools, a sudden severe headache or new confusion, vision changes or trouble speaking require urgent care. After a significant head injury, patients should seek medical evaluation, even if they initially feel fine, experts note. 5. Taking part in high-risk activities TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ A hard hit or fall can lead to serious bleeding in patients taking a blood thinner, which is why Hurts cannot play football during treatment. Patients should ask their doctor which activities are safe for them. Some may be able to continue exercising but contact sports and other activities with a high risk of injury warrant extra caution. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Blood thinners do not dissolve an existing clot, Lombardi cautioned. They help prevent it from growing while the body clears it over time. The right treatment and precautions vary, so patients should contact their care team with questions about doses, side effects or activity.

articles.title: Máxima preocupación por el estado de salud del entrenador de Luis Díaz, Vincent Kompany, tras desplomarse
articles.standfirst: El delicado estado de salud del entrenador de Luis Díaz, Vincent Kompany: hospitalizado tras desplomarse en el entrenamiento del Bayern
articles.summary: El delicado estado de salud del entrenador de Luis Díaz, Vincent Kompany: hospitalizado tras desplomarse en el entrenamiento del Bayern
articles.body: El mundo del fútbol ha recibido un serio aviso sobre la exigencia extrema del deporte de élite. Vincent Kompany, técnico de Luis Díaz en el Bayern de Múnich, se derrumbó de manera imprevista en el centro deportivo del club mientras seguía la sesión de entrenamiento del equipo filial. Tras el susto, el entrenador belga fue trasladado de urgencia a un centro hospitalario, donde se encuentra estable y bajo supervisión médica constante. El director deportivo del club bávaro, Max Eberl, compareció ante los medios de comunicación para ofrecer un parte oficial sobre el estado de salud de Kompany y explicar los detalles del incidente. "Lo más importante es que está estable. Obviamente, fue un momento difícil para todos nosotros. Se derrumbó en el campo ayer y ahora está en el hospital, donde permanecerá unos días más mientras establecen exactamente qué pasó, realizan todos los exámenes y revisan todo a fondo", declaró Eberl visiblemente afectado. El directivo aprovechó para recordar que, por encima de la alta competición y los resultados deportivos, la prioridad absoluta es el bienestar físico y mental de las personas: "Esto solo demuestra una vez más que el fútbol no es lo más importante en la vida. Lo más importante es tu salud". Eberl reconoció que el club debe asumir el reto de proteger al entrenador de su propia ética laboral, ya que el belga destaca por ser un trabajador incansable que tiende a forzar sus propios límites: Mientras los especialistas médicos completan las pruebas necesarias para determinar con exactitud las causas del desvanecimiento, el equipo se prepara para sus próximos compromisos en la Bundesliga. Desde el club se ha hecho un llamamiento a la calma y a respetar la privacidad de Kompany y su entorno, señalando que la mejor medicina en estos momentos es mantener la unidad y dedicarle una victoria sobre el terreno de juego.

articles.title: Biosimilar drugs breaking high-cost barrier to cancer immunotherapy
articles.summary: Biosimilar nivolumab is boosting access to cancer immunotherapy in India, cutting per-cycle costs from Rs 1 lakh+ to ~Rs 30,000; more price caps planned.
articles.body: MUMBAI: A quiet shift is underway in cancer care in India. Over the past six months, more patients have been prescribed immunotherapy, one of the newer advances in cancer treatment that has remained beyond the reach of many because of its prohibitive cost.The change has been driven mainly by the availability of a cheaper version of nivolumab, a key immunotherapy drug that Tata Memorial Centre (TMC) doctors say is “effective in 25 tumours and has about 100 indications”. Another factor is Indian research, including studies by TMC, suggesting that lower doses may work well in Indian patients in certain settings, potentially reducing treatment costs.Dr Imran Shaikh of Kokilaben Dhirubhai Ambani Hospital in Andheri says his prescriptions for nivolumab have risen by more than 50% in the past six months following the arrival of a cheaper biosimilar.“My patients are responding well to the drug. People who were earlier unsure whether they could afford a cycle costing over a lakh of rupees are comfortable with the new price tag of Rs 30,000,” Dr Shaikh told TOI.While it is too early to quantify the overall increase in prescriptions, the access gap has been stark. In 2022, only 2.8% of patients eligible for immunotherapy were receiving it, according to a TMC study. Dr Jyoti Bajpai, director of precision oncology at Apollo Hospitals in Navi Mumbai, who co-authored the study while at TMC, says there has been a “substantial increase” in prescriptions.Dr Kumar Prabhash, head of medical oncology at Tata Memorial Hospital in Parel, points to the gains immunotherapy has brought in some cancers, particularly melanoma, or skin cancer.“Earlier barely five out of 100 patients had long-term survival, but survival has now increased to 50% with immunotherapy,” said Dr Kumar, adding that some patients diagnosed with advanced lung cancer are now living for five years or longer.MSI-high colorectal cancer is another example of where immunotherapy can offer an alternative to conventional treatment in selected patients. “A patient of MSI-high type of colon cancer would earlier need chemotherapy, radiotherapy and surgery. But if he comes in early stages, then only immunotherapy works. The patient will have his native organ intact,” said Dr Kumar.A price cut is not enoughDespite the progress, India lags behind some countries in the availability of checkpoint inhibitors. Dr Shaikh said India offers only seven such drugs, compared with 35 in China. Apart from nivolumab, he said, the other six available in India are imported and can cost lakhs of rupees for a course of treatment.But the cost of cancer treatment could come down further following National Pharmaceutical Pricing Authority’s move, effective Nov 8, to cap trade margins on 137 anti-cancer medicines. The measure is projected to generate annual savings of Rs 2,500 crore and could offer relief across a range of treatments.But lower prices may not automatically translate into savings for patients. K M Gopakumar of Third World Network cautioned that hospitals that require patients to purchase medicines through their own pharmacies may have little incentive to stock cheaper alternatives.“Hospitals may favour more expensive original medicines because of higher margins. The cheaper versions may thus not be available to the patients as a result,” he said.Four more versions of nivolumab are expected to enter the market soon, potentially driving prices down further. “The price of the drug may drop from Rs 30,000 now to Rs 10,000, but will any place stock medicines that offer them lower margin?” he said.Dr Kumar said it remained to be seen whether the benefits of lower prices would reach patients. “We at Tata Memorial Centre make arrangements in such a way that patients have to pay the least for medicines,” he said.For Dr Bajpai, the real test is whether advances in medical and precision oncology reach patients regardless of their ability to pay. Cheaper biosimilars and evidence-based dosing strategies offer a way forward, but their promise will be realised only if lower costs translate into meaningful access to treatment.“The real success of innovation is not just how long patients live, but how many patients can access the treatment they need — without financial hardship,” said Dr Bajpai.Immunotherapy, however, is not a magic bullet. Its effectiveness varies according to the cancer type, stage and individual patient.“No medicine will work on all patients. Every medicine has indications in which it works and others in which it does not. Ditto with checkpoint inhibitors and other immunotherapy drugs,” said Dr Kumar.“Our research into short-course and low-dose approaches reflects the difficult choices patients face when cost becomes a barrier. With more affordable biosimilars, we have an opportunity to move towards evidence-based, full-dose, full-course treatment for many more eligible patients,” said Dr Bajpai.You Can Also Check: Gold Rate in Mumbai | Silver Rate in Mumbai | Bank Holidays in Mumbai | Public Holidays in Mumbai | Mumbai AQI | Weather in Mumbai | Petrol Price in Mumbai | Diesel Price in Mumbai | CNG Price in Mumbai | LPG Price in MumbaiStay updated with the latest Mumbai news. The fall came hours after Flair announced that he would be unable to attend a scheduled appearance in Seattle due to a blood clot in his leg. "My Doctors Have Limited My Travel To 3–4 Hours. Seattle Falls Outside That Range, And As Disappointed As I Am, I Have To Put My Health And Recovery First. Blood Clots Are Extremely Serious And Can Be Life-Threatening," Flair said on X. "We Have Seen This Recently With Jalen Hurts And The Complications Involving Blood Clots In His Lungs. It Is A Reminder That This Is Not Something To Take Lightly, And I Must Follow Medical Advice." Flair said he is slated to have surgery on the affected vein, "[w]hich My Doctors Expect Will Allow Me To Be Cleared For More Travel Afterward." EX-WRESTLER PAC'S SUDDEN DEATH CAUSE REVEALED BY COOK COUNTY MEDICAL EXAMINER'S OFFICE "Please Know This Decision Was Not Made Lightly. I Am Truly Sorry For The Inconvenience And Disappointment, And I Am Incredibly Grateful For Your Patience, Understanding, And Continued Support. I Look Forward To Getting Healthy And Seeing You All Down The Road. Thank You For The Love And Support," Flair added. Flair, 77, has battled health and alcohol issues over the years. Flair has been in and out of wrestling for the last few years. His so-called "Last Match"took place in 2022 — a tag-team match with his then-son-in-law, the wrestler known as Andrade, against Jeff Jarrett and Jay Lethal. He later revealed he passed out twice during the match. Flair made his All Elite Wrestling debut in 2023 and was a brief part of Sting’s final professional match at AEW Revolution, where Sting and Darby Allin took on the Young Bucks. He was a World Championship Wrestling world heavyweight champion eight times, a National Wrestling Alliance world heavyweight champion nine times and a WWE champion twice during his career. articles.title: Abercynon woman, 93, waits 10 hours on floor for an ambulance
articles.summary: Graham Anthony says his mum Margaret Owen was asking for help "and sometimes screaming in pain".
articles.body:
A 93-year-old woman had to lie on the floor for 10-and-a-half hours with broken bones while waiting for an ambulance.

Margaret Owen fell in her home on 4 October and her son Graham Anthony went over after getting a call from her lifeline alarm at 06:15.

He said an ambulance was called at 07:35, but a St John Ambulance worker only came at the request of the Welsh Ambulance Service at 15:30.

It was another 90 minutes until an ambulance came and took Margaret to hospital.

"Listening to her repeatedly asking for help and sometimes screaming in pain has left me with a feeling of hopelessness," said Graham.

Welsh Ambulance Service boss Lee Brooks said he was sorry to hear about Margaret's experience.

Anthony said his mum, from Abercynon, Rhondda Cynon Taf, has dementia and struggled to remember exactly what happened.

"I don't know how long she was on the floor for before she activated the alarm," he said.

"She was obviously in clear distress on the floor... her right leg was immobilised, and she was complaining of pain in her right arm.

Margaret suffered fractures to her femur and shoulder and needed surgery, but is yet to leave Royal Glamorgan Hospital.

While Anthony praised the professionalism of the ambulance crew who responded and said they dealt with his mum "really well", he admitted the experience "knocked my confidence in our health service's ability to respond".

According to the latest published figures, 10,977 patients waited 12 hours or more for an ambulance in August, 733 (6.3%) fewer than the previous month.

Anthony put a post on Facebook page sharing his mother's experience, saying the delay was not acceptable "for anyone, let alone a 93-year-old".

He said the response "has been huge", with hundreds of people sharing their experiences of elderly relatives going through similar waits for medical care.

The Welsh government said it recognised how distressing it could be to wait for care when someone has suffered an injury and that improving access to care was a "key priority".

It added that a new emergency and acute care policy framework would be published this autumn, setting out how plans to improve emergency community response and hospital flow.

"It's not a service, is it really? It's a huge systemic problem and nobody seems to be getting to grips with it," Anthony said.

"It's a terrible indictment on the health service and nobody seems to be getting to grips with it.

"There are far too many examples of similar injuries, similar waits," he said.

Anthony said he had submitted a formal complaint to the Welsh Ambulance Service and the Welsh government.

Brooks, the ambulance service's chief operating officer, said he was "grateful" to have the incident brought to his attention.

"Waiting almost eight hours for help is not the standard of service we want to provide," he added.

He said a preliminary review identified "aspects" of the way the call was managed that require further investigation and staff were looking "carefully" at what happened to understand if there were opportunities to respond differently.

In July 2025, NHS Wales re-categorised ambulance calls - purple for cardiac or respiratory arrest and red for major trauma and other emergencies where patients risk cardiac or respiratory arrest.

In December, three new categories were introduced - orange for serious conditions, yellow for people who need to be assessed and green for less urgent.

According to NHS activity and performance data for the past two months, the median ambulance response times for red calls was nine minutes and 32 seconds - missing the target of six to eight minutes.

The median response for purple calls was seven minutes and 31 seconds - within target.

For orange calls, the median response time increased to nearly one hour 30 minutes, up from about one hour.

The category's lengthiest response time period, since records began last December, was in January at one hour and 53 minutes.

Data on response times for yellow and green calls, and the response time target for orange calls, are not published publicly.

In September, the ambulance service received 11,868 orange calls, 5,492 yellow calls and 1,414 green calls.

articles.body:
Hospital São João Batista, em Volta Redonda — Foto: Divulgação/Cris Oliveira

Um jovem, de 22 anos, ficou ferido após sofrer um ataque a tiros neste domingo (25) em Piraí (RJ). O caso aconteceu no distrito de Arrozal.

Segundo a Polícia Militar , os agentes foram acionados no Hospital São João Batista, em Volta Redonda (RJ), após o jovem dar entrada com ferimentos a bala.

Ainda de acordo com a corporação, em depoimento aos agentes, o ferido afirmou que estava em um estabelecimento comercial quando foi atacado com cinco disparos. O ferido foi atingido em ambas as pernas, na região da coxa. Ele foi atendido e liberado pela unidade médica.

Além dele, o jovem também informou que seu amigo também foi baleado e socorrido na Unidade Básica de Saúde de Arrozal.

O caso foi registrado na delegacia de Volta Redonda.

A identidade dele não foi divulgada pela Polícia Militar.

Até o momento da publicação desta reportagem ninguém havia sido preso.
