articles.title: Usman Khawaja reveals secret battle with rheumatoid arthritis during his cricket career: Early symptoms, causes, risk factors, and more
articles.summary: Aussie cricketer Usman Khawaja spent nearly his whole international Test cricket career carrying a secret: he was living with rheumatoid arthritis, a
articles.body: Aussie cricketer Usman Khawaja spent nearly his whole international Test cricket career carrying a secret: he was living with rheumatoid arthritis, a relentless autoimmune disease that once left him barely able to shuffle from his bed to the bathroom. He kept this battle hidden for years, worried that being open about his diagnosis could cost him his cricketing dreams, or make others see him differently. Only after he hung up his baggy green following Australia’s Ashes win in January 2026 did he decide it was time to share his story.Usman Khawaja’s revelation: What the cricketer sharedIn his interview with the Australian Broadcasting Corporation’s Australian Story, published recently, Usman Khawaja talked about those early, terrifying days. The pain in his left knee was so excruciating he actually wondered if he was dying. Imagine being a young athlete with your whole future ahead of you and, suddenly, you can’t walk the ten metres to the bathroom. That’s exactly where Khawaja was at just 22: stuck, scared, and unsure if he’d ever set foot on a cricket field again.But Usman is no quitter; he fought back. Through a mix of stubborn persistence, medical support, and regular injections of medication, he managed to claw his way back into cricket about six months after being diagnosed. He describes the medication as a “godsend”—he honestly believes without it, he would have had to say goodbye to the game, and maybe even to a normal life. Treatment didn’t make things easy, but it gave him a fighting chance. In the end, he played 88 Tests, scored over 6,000 runs, and notched up 16 centuries.His decision to reveal his struggles now has put a spotlight on rheumatoid arthritis, a disease people often think only bothers older folks or is just a part of getting old. That’s not true. Rheumatoid arthritis is actually much messier: it’s a harsh autoimmune disorder that can cripple people of all ages, stealing their energy, damaging their joints, and even affecting organs beyond bones and cartilage.What exactly is rheumatoid arthritis?It’s a condition where your own immune system turns against you, attacking the tissue lining your joints. This inflames the joints, making them hurt, swell, and stiffen up. For some, the damage isn’t just in the hands and feet, but goes after places like the heart, lungs, or eyes.The World Health Organization says about 18 million people worldwide had it in 2019. Some get lucky and experience stretches of relief, but for others, the pain and fatigue just keep coming back, making work, sleep, and even basic chores tough. Without treatment, the inflammation sticks around and can permanently wreck your joints.Khawaja’s story brings home how brutal the disease can be. If a fit, professional athlete can be floored by it, what about everyday people?The early signsFor rheumatoid arthritis, the signs often start subtly. You might feel joint pain, especially after resting, or stiffness in the morning that lasts longer than you’d expect with regular aches. Joints get swollen, warm, and tender, sometimes on both sides of the body (like both wrists). Persistent fatigue is common, too. Sometimes you get hit with a low-grade fever or lose your appetite. Everyday stuff, like opening jars, climbing stairs, or even dressing, starts to feel like a marathon. Symptoms can come and go, and just when you think you’re improving, a flare-up can knock you back again.If you notice lasting swelling, pain, or your mornings turn into a stiff battle, don’t brush it off. These signs don’t always mean you have rheumatoid arthritis, but it’s worth seeing a professional healthcare provider. Catching it early can really help limit the damage.Why does rheumatoid arthritis hit some people and not others?Nobody’s completely sure. Scientists suspect a mix of genes and environmental triggers. Well-known risk factors include smoking, being female, getting older, and having a family member with the disease. Obesity and certain pollutants can also raise the risk. But you can still get it even if you tick none of those boxes. Khawaja was just 22, and a living proof that it can strike younger adults.What about prevention?At the moment, there’s no foolproof way to avoid getting rheumatoid arthritis. You can stack the odds in your favour by staying active, eating well, keeping your weight healthy, avoiding cigarettes, and even caring for your teeth. None of these guarantee you won’t get it, but they support general health and might help.Diagnosing it isn’t straightforward, since the symptoms often masquerade as other problems. Doctors usually check your history, examine aching joints, and run blood tests looking for inflammation and specific antibodies. Imaging like X-rays or ultrasounds can reveal damage. But there’s no single test that says “you’ve got RA.” Rheumatologists piece together clues from different sources.Is there a cure for RA?As for treatment, the goal isn’t to cure but to manage. Doctors usually prescribe drugs called DMARDs (like methotrexate) or newer biologicals to slow the disease. You might take anti-inflammatory meds or painkillers, along with therapies to keep you moving and able to handle day-to-day tasks. Khawaja credits his return to cricket to regular medication injections, though he hasn’t named the drug, so speculation isn’t helpful. What matters is that treatment must be personal, tailored to each patient, and always guided by medical professionals.Despite the severity of his illness, Khawaja didn’t let it define him. Two years after diagnosis, he debuted in Test cricket and went on to achieve greatness, eventually retiring a hero after the Ashes in 2026. By sharing his story now, he wants to give hope to others fighting autoimmune diseases, showing them that a difficult diagnosis doesn’t always spell the end of their ambitions.Get the latest movie news, reviews, and celebrity updates. articles.title: Hansi Flick, entrenador del Barcelona: "Me despierto sobre las cinco y media de la mañana, desayuno avena con frutas y hago deporte todos los días"
articles.standfirst: El técnico alemán mantiene una rutina estricta
articles.summary: El técnico alemán mantiene una rutina estricta
articles.body: Este domingo, 25 de octubre, es una jornada especial, ya que el FC Barcelona afronta ‘El Clásico’ de LaLiga contra el Real Madrid. Sin embargo, para el entrenador azulgrana Hansi Flick habrá sido un día más en su estricta rutina, pues siempre arranca su día con una seria disciplina marcada por un desayuno saludable y ejercicio diario desde las 5:30 de la mañana. “Me despierto sobre las cinco y media de la mañana, desayuno avena con frutas y hago deporte todos los días”, confesó. En primer lugar, Fick tiene una puntualidad sagrada y es inflexible con los horarios; de hecho, es de los primeros en llegar a la Ciudad Deportiva del Barça. Las sesiones de activación previas a los partidos en la mañana de partido son obligatorias al minuto. Sobre lo que toma al empezar el día, el entrenador desayuna meticulosamente avena con frutas. “Es lo que me da energía estable. Y, por supuesto, mucho café. Bebo mucho café durante la mañana; es mi combustible para las primeras reuniones con el staff”, apuntaba. Además, vigila de cerca la alimentación y suplementación de la plantilla junto a los especialistas del club. Asimismo, el alemán de 61 años también incluye en deporte en su rutina. “Si mi cuerpo está activo, mi mente está rápida. Les pido intensidad a ellos, así que yo tengo que ser el primero en mostrar esa energía”, señalaba, asegurando que ha impuesto rutinas físicas de hasta dos horas de alta intensidad a su plantilla para sostener el ritmo que pide. De esta manera, su exigencia coincide con lo que sus jugadores hacen en el campo. Finalmente, Flick resume por qué es tan estricto con estos horarios y hábitos con una frase que ya se ha hecho famosa en el vestuario. “La disciplina no es un castigo, es un estilo de vida. Si controlas tu mañana, controlas tu día. Y si controlas tu día, tienes más opciones de ganar el fin de semana”, sentenció.

articles.title: Can a viral diabetes cure do more harm than good? Doctor warns how misleading claims about diets, supplements and natural remedies can prompt patients to stop medication, disrupt blood sugar control and risk serious complications
articles.summary: Taking your tablets and checking your sugar is only part of living with diabetes.
articles.body: Taking your tablets and checking your sugar is only part of living with diabetes. Every day you also decide what to eat, what to trust, and whether the medicine is even necessary. Increasingly, those decisions are being shaped by a reel, a wellness influencer or a forwarded message promising a natural fix.The trouble starts when one of those claims changes what a person actually does. Skipping a dose, dropping a food group or trying an unproven remedy may feel small at first.Why the cure claims landThe posts are easy to find: a special diet, a herbal drink, a supplement, a kitchen remedy, sometimes with the promise that diabetes can be reversed without a doctor. For anyone tired of daily pills or frightened of complications, that is a tempting pitch.But controlling blood sugar and curing diabetes are different things. Some people with type 2 diabetes do reach remission under specific conditions, yet remission is not a permanent cure. People with type 1 diabetes need insulin, full stop.Dr Santosh Kumar Agrawal, Director of Internal Medicine at Yatharth Super Speciality Hospital, Sector 88, Faridabad, told TOI that misinformation can push people toward unsafe practices or make them delay treatment they need. Some stop their medicines or insulin after reading about an alternative, he said. Sugar then runs uncontrolled, and the heart, kidneys, eyes and nerves are put at greater risk.The false claim is not the only problem. The bigger one is when it takes the place of a plan built around one person’s condition.One formula doesn’t fit everyoneWhat works for one person may do nothing for another. Type of diabetes, age, other illnesses, activity levels and current medication all matter. Online advice ignores that. One video calls a common food poison, the next calls it a miracle, and a third says you can stop your medicines once your numbers look good.Dr Agrawal warned that such messages set unrealistic expectations and lead people to try diets or supplements without weighing the risks.Comparing your readings with a friend’s, or with strangers online, adds needless worry too. A number that suits one person may be the wrong target for another, and that target should come from your doctor. The US CDC’s diabetes pages make the same point: care should be individual, combining treatment, healthy eating and physical activity. No single food, routine or supplement replaces that.“Natural” is not the same as safeA plant-based label makes a product sound gentler than a prescription. It isn’t necessarily. Herbal preparations and supplements can interact with prescribed drugs, and their ingredients and strength vary from one product to the next. Using one in place of proven treatment can also delay getting sugar under control.Lifestyle changes do matter: balanced meals, regular exercise, enough sleep and a healthy weight all help, and under medical supervision they can bring some people with type 2 diabetes into remission. That still isn’t a reason to stop medication on your own.Dr Agrawal’s advice is to talk to your doctor before acting on anything seen online, especially if you take insulin or medicines that can push sugar too low. Changing meals, fasting or doses can shift glucose levels quickly.Food myths, fasting and readings without contextMisinformation also shapes how people eat and monitor. Rigid food rules can lead someone to avoid perfectly nutritious foods. Others do the opposite and eat a “diabetic-friendly” snack without checking the carbohydrates or the portion.Fasting is another risk. Anyone on insulin or certain tablets can slip into low blood sugar if they fast without adjusting their plan. Highs can follow too, when people misread how meals, illness, stress or medication affect glucose.A single reading says little on its own. Doctors look at patterns, symptoms, medicines and tests such as HbA1c. The NIDDK offers reliable information on management, glucose monitoring and treatment, though decisions should still go through your care team.Spotting bad adviceBe wary when a post:Promises a permanent cureTells you to stop prescribed medicinesPresents one food as a complete treatmentSays a supplement works for everyoneLeans on dramatic testimonials rather than evidenceA success story may be true, but it doesn’t show the method is safe or effective for anyone else. Before changing anything, check whether the source is a recognised medical body or a qualified professional, and ask your doctor or a registered dietitian about anything confusing.Good diabetes care takes more than discipline. It means knowing whose advice to trust. A question asked at your next appointment is a far safer move than a decision made after a 30-second video.Medical experts consultedThis article includes expert inputs shared with TOI Health by:Dr Santosh Kumar Agrawal, Director - Internal Medicine, Yatharth Super Speciality Hospital Faridabad Sector 88.Inputs highlight how false claims about diabetes cures, diets can mislead patients, disrupt treatment and increase health risks, stressing the importance of seeking medical advice before trying alternative remedies or changing prescribed medication.

articles.title: Selena Gomez's vaping admission highlights hidden health risks doctors say millions face daily
articles.summary: Selena Gomez called vaping "stupid" after it altered her voice, but doctors warn the health risks go beyond vocal cord damage for millions.
articles.body: When Selena Gomez revealed to her millions of followers that heavy nicotine vaping had noticeably altered her voice, calling the habit "stupid," her confession highlighted a larger issue with the practice. For the singer and actress, the physical toll manifested in her vocal cords. But medical professionals emphasize that her experience is only a visible symptom of a deeper health crisis affecting millions of Americans who use e-cigarettes every day. While often marketed as a safer alternative to conventional cigarettes, e-cigarettes pose significant health risks. Aside from the immediate vocal strain and airway inflammation noted by otolaryngologists, major health institutions warn that regular vaping exposes the body to a cocktail of toxic chemicals, cardiovascular strain and respiratory risks. SELENA GOMEZ WARNS FANS AFTER VAPING HABIT LEAVES HER WITH PERMANENT CONSEQUENCE Specialists emphasize that e-cigarettes deliver more concentrated doses of nicotine than traditional cigarettes, rapidly driving chemical dependency in the brain. "With e-cigarettes and vaping, you can get a very high dose of nicotine, and that directly correlates to addiction and how difficult it can be to break these patterns," Trent Carter, a nurse practitioner and CEO of Renew Health in New Mexico, previously told Fox News Digital. Carter notes that high nicotine intake without traditional smoke can carry its own health consequences. "It can lead to sleep disturbances, increased anxiety, and if you have underlying cardiac problems or high blood pressure, it’s going to raise your heart rate and elevate your blood pressure, leading to all sorts of issues." According to the American Lung Association, the aerosol produced by e-cigarettes contains fine chemical particles, heavy metals such as nickel and lead, and organic compounds. Over time, inhaling these irritants can trigger chronic airway inflammation, irreversible lung tissue scarring, and obstructive pulmonary conditions. NEVER SMOKED A CIGARETTE? YOU COULD STILL BE AT HIGHER RISK FOR LUNG CANCER A major concern among physicians is the chemical composition of e-liquids. Even nicotine-free formulas contain flavorings and solvent agents like propylene glycol and vegetable glycerin. When heated by the device’s coil, these liquids break down into toxic compounds, including formaldehyde and acrolein, both known to damage cellular structures in the respiratory system. Doctors stress that because modern e-cigarettes have only been widely used for a little over a decade, long-term health consequences are still unclear. While immediate effects may appear as hoarseness, coughing, or reduced athletic endurance, the larger impact poses risks to long-term vital organ function. For many attempting to quit vaping, traditional tools like nicotine patches or gum can fall short because they don't address the psychological habit. TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ "While a patch or gum can help with physical cravings, if you aren't addressing the behavioral aspect, you're missing a huge component," Carter said. CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER "Vaping can become constant throughout the day. Subconsciously, you might not even realize how frequently you're doing it, or that you're using it to cope with underlying anxiety or lack of sleep."
